cross_market_insights: Sydney and Brisbane share the same weak top 3 pattern: an unreadable university record, an official Indonesian-language PDF, and an unsourced Instagram post. No page in the top 3 is written for an Australian couple.

No ranking page states the rule as the Australian Embassy words it, links the official law text, or pairs it with the Australian-side steps (CNI from the Consulate-General in Bali, recognition per Smartraveller and AGD).

Interfaith content is academic (ResearchGate) or a law-firm blog; nobody turns the official texts (Law No. 1 of 1974, Constitutional Court rulings, SEMA 2/2023) into a plain, neutral summary for foreign couples.
Travel-site snippets carry an outdated minimum marriage age; an accurate, dated, official-source page has a real trust gap to win.

People Also Ask leans to 'Is a wedding in Bali legal in Australia?' (both markets) and 'Is religion required for marriage?' and 'requirements of a civil marriage' (Brisbane). These map directly to FAQ and H2s.
Search volume is tiny or unreported for every variant; this is a cluster-completeness and trust piece, not a traffic piece. Win the AI overview and PAA with clean, quotable sentences.

Own site already answers fragments (Bali hub, cost-to-elope-in-bali, ultimate Bali guide, 2024 tips post); none owns the religion requirement. The ultimate Bali guide's snippet ('Both a religious and civil ceremony must occur at the same location on the same day') is unsourced and should be checked against official sources (SITE-CONFLICTS).
payload.recommended_angle: The only page that states Bali's religion requirement exactly as the Australian Embassy and Law No. 1 of 1974 do, lists recognised religions from an official list only, summarises what official texts say for couples of different faiths or no faith without opinion, and then shows the route many Australian couples take: marry legally at home, celebrate in Bali, with a Wedded Advisor handling the Bali week.
